1:
Every voice begins by noting that the chapter is out of place. John Gill observes that the prophecy belongs to the siege under Zedekiah, while chapters that follow it were delivered under Jehoiakim and Jeconiah, who both reigned earlier. Adam Clarke says the remaining chapters seem strangely interchanged, dates this discourse to about the ninth year of Zedekiah, and passes on an ordering in which it stands first among the prophecies delivered after the revolt. Charles Ellicott calls it an obvious gap in the collection and the opening of a new group running to the close of the thirty-third chapter, the earlier work being the roll read before Jehoiakim and this the roll of Zedekiah. Keil and Delitzsch divide the same body differently, into judgment on Judah and the nations through the twenty-ninth chapter and restoration in the four that follow, and note that these prophecies are marked off by headings giving occasion and date.

On the two messengers they agree and add to each other. Gill, Clarke, Ellicott and John Calvin all say that this Pashur is not the priest of the previous chapter, that one being son of Immer and this one son of Melchiah. Matthew Henry notes that the two belonged to different courses of the priesthood, the fifth and the twenty-fourth; Ellicott makes the first the head of his family or course and the second the deputy or second priest. Henry thinks it was well that the king sent, and sent men of rank, but better if he had asked a conference in person, which he might easily have had; and he observes that priests no better than the rest were now commanded to carry a respectful message, a mortification to them and an honour to the prophet who had lately said his days were consumed with shame.

What the embassy was really after divides them. Calvin insists on its good faith: they did not flatter the prophet so as to draw a false answer out of him but wished God to be consulted, which shows they were convinced of his integrity and knew he would say nothing from himself. Ellicott reads it as a trap. The messengers come to enquire and yet suggest the answer they expect, the deliverance of the city as when an Assyrian army perished before it; and he takes the whole for an attempt, under a show of devout reverence, to entice Jeremiah into changing his tone and siding with the war policy, adding that these two are found later ready to accuse him of being a traitor.

Zedekiah himself is measured the same way by three voices. Henry charges him with humbling himself only when necessity forced it, and so far as to want the prophet’s help but not so far as to take his advice. Calvin calls him neither one of the worst nor a man who feared God, but as it were neutral, keeping a half-buried fear of religion that never bore any weight, and adds that many such are found still. John Wesley puts it in one line, that he was none of the best and none of the worst of the kings. Henry sharpens it from what they ask: all their care is to be rid of their trouble rather than at peace with God, so that they pray the enemy may go up from them and not that their God may return, like Pharaoh asking only that this death be taken away. Calvin finds the same fault in the reasoning: Zedekiah assumes that the covenant stands, which is true, but the application is false, since covenant-breakers were pleading a covenant they had made void. Ellicott notes that the spelling of the name here is the more correct one, as one would expect from a writer who had met the man and his officers, and reports four proposed meanings for it.
3:
Before the answer itself John Calvin notices how it was delivered. The prophet did not go to the king in person but sent the message back by the messengers, and Calvin thinks this deliberate and prompted by the Spirit: not that he despised his king, but that a pride which had treated God very insolently had to be cast down, so that the king might know whom he was dealing with. The title under which the answer comes is turned against the men who asked for it. John Gill says the God of Israel had been and still was and would be Israel God, the God of such as are Israelites indeed, though he gave up this generation to ruin, so that it was vain to hope anything from a name they merely bore. Calvin makes the same point against what Zedekiah had urged: the wonderful works he leaned on did not belong to him, and if God destroyed him and all his people he would still not be inconsistent with himself or depart from his covenant.

The weapons that are turned back are read three ways. Adam Clarke takes the promise simply, that every attempt to repel the Chaldeans will fail and the city will be delivered into their hands. Charles Ellicott works on the word order and finds siegecraft in it: the phrase about being outside the walls belongs not to the besiegers but to the fighting, so that the defenders are driven back from their outer line of fortifications within the gates, the enemy pressing nearer until they are inside. Calvin prefers a third sense. The verb he renders I prohibit, so that however well furnished the city may be with weapons and forces, God forbids their use and makes them avail nothing; he reports that some render it I will turn them against you, and that the root carries the ideas of turning aside and changing, which he thinks points to turning a thing to a contrary purpose. Keil and Delitzsch keep the received rendering and add the summary that God is about to make his almighty power known, but not for rescue.

On God fighting in person the two who comment are agreed and appalled. Gill draws the contrast with what was asked: so far from acting as their friend according to his wondrous works, he sets himself against them as their enemy, which is more terrible than the whole Chaldean army with the king of Babylon at its head, since if God be for a people none can hurt them and if he is against them it signifies nothing who is for them. Calvin says the same in military terms: God is the leader of this war and the Chaldeans are as it were his hired soldiers, waiting for his signal; the fathers found that power employed for their safety, and this generation will learn by experience how great it is to destroy.

The three words for anger Calvin takes as a deliberate climb. The first means simply wrath, the second heated wrath, the third foaming wrath with great added to it; and only one of the old versions, he notes, preserves the ascent, two of them reducing three terms to two. The gradation answers to the provocations, and the point of piling them up is that God means to be understood as implacable, so that Zedekiah may not go on thinking the end of his troubles near. Calvin closes with a defence of the severity. The prophet had not laid down his office nor shut out repentance, but the king could not be awakened otherwise, and this opening was meant to fall like a thunderclap; men grown torpid in their evils and then so obstinate that they tried to subject God to themselves had to see that they were wholly lost before any offer of mercy could reach them.
6:
The pestilence draws two accounts of how such a thing is to be read. Adam Clarke separates it from the sword: the sword may look like the work of men, even though the Chaldeans hold their commission from God, but the pestilence will appear as his immediate act. Charles Ellicott grants the natural cause first, saying that plague was doubtless the ordinary consequence of a siege, as ancient historians record elsewhere, and then adds that it came before the people as one more proof that the arm of God was stretched out against them, so that they were fighting that arm as well as the host outside; he notes that the outstretched hand is a phrase carried over from the older law. John Calvin presses the divine authorship hardest, observing that God assumes to himself what might have been credited to the Chaldeans, and warns that even if the besiegers failed to storm the city its ruin would be worse, since famine and plague would consume it from within.

That the beasts die with the men is left to Calvin alone. It is no wonder, he says, that the vengeance should reach horses and oxen and asses, since all of them were made for the use of man; but he will not pretend the animals deserve it, and asks outright how we can suppose that a horse or an ass had earned death by disease or by want of daily food. The spectacle is set up, he answers, to touch men more effectually, so that seeing innocent creatures caught in the same punishment they may understand that the whole world lies under a curse through their sins, the ground failing of its increase and the very air turning deadly. John Gill reads the threat more narrowly, taking those who are smitten to be those who abide in the city and will not go out and surrender.

The seventh verse is where Calvin says the last hope is taken away. Sieges are often raised, he observes, when the besieged are so obstinate that they master famine and thirst, until the men outside think they are fighting wild beasts and go away; here the event will be otherwise, and the endurance will simply be wasted, the survivors being handed over at the end of it. He notes that the king is named on purpose, so that the people may not comfort themselves that they are safe under his shadow, and that the servants named beside him are the counsellors and courtiers, men full of pride and very hostile to the prophets, blinded by their own wisdom. He takes the following clause to mean even the residue, the point being that Jerusalem was populous when this was spoken, so that after God had reduced the people to a remnant there would still be no end of their evils. The repetition about being given into the hand of their enemies he refuses to call superfluous: the Chaldeans would not be satisfied with plunder or make any account of silver and gold, but would come burning to shed blood, as another prophet says of them.

On the name of the conqueror Clarke counts the spellings, one form standing in twenty-six places of this book and the other in ten, the difference being a single letter, with the manuscripts divided and the same man meant either way. Ellicott ends on what it cost to say this. The words were bold ones to utter while the king was still on his throne and was being urged on by his princes to defy the king of Babylon, and he points to the close of the book for their literal fulfilment.
8:
The offer of two ways is recognised by all as a bitter quotation. Matthew Henry says the law and the prophets had long set life and death before this people in another sense, life on obedience; they slighted that life, so the words now denote not a fair proposal but a melancholy dilemma, two evils of which they must choose the less, and the less is a shameful captivity, all the life left them to propose. Charles Ellicott calls it a solemn irony, the phrase being taken here in its lowest and most literal sense: the way of life is no longer the way of righteousness leading to eternal blessedness but simply submission to the Chaldeans, and the life so gained is one of exile and poverty if not bondage. John Calvin makes the same distinction and adds the reason: since the Chaldeans fight under the authority of God, resistance could succeed only by overcoming God himself, so that the one hope left is to acknowledge a just judgment and bear exile with a resigned mind. Henry notes that the advice was hateful to men whom false prophets had flattered into holding out, and that a foreign envoy once urged the same surrender in vain while God was still on their side.

What the advice sounded like, and whether anyone took it, they answer differently. Ellicott says the words must have seemed to counsel treachery, and were thrown back at the prophet in a later taunt, but that not a few in fact acted on them. Henry says the opposite: for aught that appears few or none took the counsel, so wretchedly were their hearts hardened to their own destruction. Calvin anticipates the objection, that to go out as a suppliant to a besieging army is to throw a life away, and answers that God would not have promised safety unless he had the Chaldeans in his power and could turn their minds as he pleased.

The verb rendered falleth Calvin turns over at length. It means strictly to fall; those who render it died, he says, touch neither heaven nor earth; the reading that makes a lot fall among brethren is unnatural; he takes it to mean dwelling, while allowing an allusion to subjection, since going over to the Chaldeans meant great reproach. He lists what the versions do with it, one having go to, another fly to, another obey, one omitting it altogether. John Gill adds that the man who abides does so imagining himself safe and not fearing the city can be taken. Keil and Delitzsch render the whole promise as having his soul for a prey.

That last phrase draws four explanations. John Wesley calls it proverbial, a man holding his own life as booty recovered from an enemy. Ellicott says it is characteristic of this prophet and illustrates the misery of the time, life being no secure possession but spoil a man snatches and hurries away with lest another take it. Calvin makes the prey an accidental gain, a thing found and carried off by stealth. Henry offers two senses at once, that the life is saved with difficulty, as a prey is taken from the mighty, and that the joy of escaping will equal the joy of those who divide the spoil; they had expected to plunder the enemy camp as their ancestors once plundered an Assyrian one. On the closing sentence Gill notes that one paraphrase reads my fury for my face; Calvin observes that the Hebrew sets the face upon the city rather than against it, and that to set the face means to be resolute; and Adam Clarke feels the weight of it for any who still reverenced the temple. Ellicott adds that burning a captured city was common but not universal, conquerors often preferring to keep the palaces they took, and suspects the answer to the messengers ended here.
11:
Whether these verses belong here is the first question. John Gill reports that some think this part was delivered earlier, before the peremptory decree went out, since a reformation is here offered some hope of pardon. Charles Ellicott says the supplied word say is not wanted and gives the wrong impression of a new message; he sets both sides out, the conditional threatening being held to imply an earlier stage than the doom just pronounced and referred to the early years of Jehoiakim, while others urge that it has the character of a last promise and so a last warning. Keil and Delitzsch name three scholars who deny any connection with what precedes and place the passage under Jehoiakim, an exhortation being out of place after an unconditional sentence. John Calvin keeps it where it stands and denies the inconsistency: though the king was to go into exile he might still obtain favour after submitting to a paternal correction. Gill notes that one version joins the phrase to the burning of the city, as though the palace were to burn with it, and insists that the house of the king means his family rather than his dwelling.

Why the name of David is used divides them sharply. Gill takes it as an appeal to example: the title reminds them of their descent and how much it became them to do justice as their ancestor did, since otherwise being his seed would not secure them. Calvin will not have it. The name is brought in not for honour but by way of reproach, and he dismisses as unmeaning the notion that David is named for his justice; the point is the covenant, which these men had turned into a private exemption because God had chosen the family and promised the kingdom. Hypocrites, he says, appropriate every promise and boast that God is bound to them without faith or repentance; so the name is thrown at them in contempt, since the covenant was made on condition of faithful service and they had grown wholly unlike their father. Matthew Henry stands nearer Calvin: their wickedness was the worse for their descent from David.

Judgment in the morning is mostly taken both ways at once. Adam Clarke thinks the morning was probably the appointed hour, when the people went out to work, but allows the words may simply mean do justice promptly. Ellicott makes it a chief duty of an eastern king, to rise at dawn and sit in the gate hearing the wronged, and finds the neglect costly: it gave an opening for the rebellion David suffered; if the king lay slothful the noon heat made the chance unrecoverable, worse still where the mornings went to revelry. Calvin allows the literal sense, noting that in corrupt times judges spent the morning drinking, and the figurative one of acting promptly. John Wesley keeps the second only, justice without partiality and done quickly.

Calvin presses two further points. The verb should be rendered defend rather than judge, and a modern rendering making it intransitive he calls inadmissible. He doubts too the distinction some draw between the two words for oppression, one for withholding wages and the other for taking by force, since the prophet uses them as a pair. The charge he states without softening: the king and his courtiers plundered freely, so that the house where the living image of God should have shone was become a house of spoils, the judges themselves associates of robbers. Yet Calvin will not let it end in despair: it is most unreasonable that the fear by which God recalls us should drive us to despair, since his wrath is not removed but mitigated, and mitigation is a great thing. Henry says the same more plainly: if God be for us, who can be against us, and if he be against us, who can do anything for us.
13:
The address is topographical and they cannot agree on the ground. Charles Ellicott splits the two phrases between the two parts of the city: the noun is feminine, and as the daughter of Zion stands for Zion, so the inhabitant of the valley is the lower city, the older prophet valley of vision, while the rock of the plain is the higher city on the hill; the people trusted, as the Jebusites had before them, in what seemed the impregnable strength of their position. He sees no reason for taking the words as a symbol of the royal house, though palaces on the hill and in the valley may have given them a pointed application. John Calvin and John Wesley keep them for one place. Calvin observes that except for the one mount the city lay in a valley ringed by mountains, so that access was difficult and the citizens took courage from the situation; Wesley says the higher mountains around made the mount itself a valley by comparison, and the city was a rock near the plain, a position that made the Jews think it could not be stormed.

How hard the phrase is may be judged from the versions Calvin reports: one gives the valley of a place named as a proper noun, another the inhabitress of the solid valley and of the plain, another one who dwells in valleys and has a large plain, and a paraphrase drops the ground for dwelling in strength in fortified cities. One scholar he cites supposed an actual valley of that name in the city. Adam Clarke reports a rendering that makes the whole the levelled hollow of a rock, and says flatly that with all its explanation he cannot see the good sense of it; his own account is that Jerusalem, though partly on two hills, ran out into the valley, while the city of David was properly a rock, fortified by nature and art and reckoned impregnable by its old possessors. John Gill works only on the opening words, which may be supplied either as behold, I say unto thee, or behold, I come unto thee.

The boast that follows is given a speaker by Clarke, who takes it for the language of the courtiers who persuaded Zedekiah to rebel against Babylon. Calvin sets the confidence in a wider frame. Jerusalem was the head and seat of all the evils of the nation, partly from more licentiousness there, partly because the citizens supposed themselves exempt by privilege from the reproof of prophets, partly from the walls and towers themselves; and he notes the change of number in the verse.

The forest that is to burn draws four explanations. Calvin rejects the reading that makes it the neighbouring towns as foreign to the sense, and allows a metaphor only for the buildings of the city, whose houses were framed of tall timber in such quantity that the mass could be called a forest; but he half prefers a simpler account, that the trees of Lebanon are meant, part of the false glory of the place, which would supply the materials for burning it. Ellicott offers both a literal woodland, then covering more ground than later, and the royal palace, known from its cedar columns as the house of the forest of Lebanon. Wesley takes both together, the forest or the houses cut out of it, and adds that the fire will not stop at the city but consume the country round. Clarke reads it as a fire set at the centre and spreading to the circumference. He notes too, as others have on this chapter, that another chapter should follow here. Calvin closes on what the passage is for: nothing is more hateful to God than false confidence, since men who promise themselves a safe condition grow torpid, despise his judgments, and end by supposing themselves outside his authority altogether.
